meta.topic: Fraud controls in real-time payment journeys

problem:
Meridian Bank offers instant payments that settle in seconds, which is exactly what customers want and exactly what fraudsters want too. A fraudster who gains access to a customer account can move money out before the customer notices, and an authorised push payment scam can persuade the customer to send the money themselves. The bank's fraud team sees the pattern in the data: new beneficiaries, unusual amounts, high velocity across accounts, logins from new devices, and payments made under time pressure.

The challenge is to stop fraud without stopping genuine payments. A control that challenges every payment will drive customers away, and a control that challenges none will let fraud through. The bank must consider risk signals, velocity, confirmation, intervention and post transaction monitoring as one journey, so the friction lands on the risky payment and not on the routine one.

The case matters because instant payments are hard to recall. Once the money has settled, recovery depends on the beneficiary bank, the scheme rules and the speed of the fraud report, so prevention and fast intervention matter far more than after the event recovery.
solution:
Score every payment in real time from a set of signals, not from a single rule. The signals include the beneficiary history, the amount against the customer profile, velocity across the account and across the bank, device and location signals, time of day, and whether the payment follows a recent change such as a new payee or a changed contact detail. Each signal contributes to a risk score, and the score drives a proportionate response: proceed, step up with additional authentication, show the verified beneficiary name and ask for explicit confirmation, hold for analyst review, or reject.

Use confirmation as a control, not as a formality. Verification of Payee, mandatory for instant euro payments from 9 October 2025, shows the customer whether the name they entered matches the account, and a mismatch or a close match must be presented clearly with a pause before the customer can proceed. Confirmation of the amount, the beneficiary and the purpose, in plain language, is the last chance to stop an authorised push payment scam, so it must never be a pre ticked box or a screen the customer can rush past.

Intervene in the journey, not only after it. A payment that exceeds the risk threshold is held with a clear status and a defined review path, and the customer is contacted through a trusted channel. The hold records the signals, the score, the threshold and the decision, so the analyst can see why the payment was stopped and the customer can understand what happened.

Monitor after the transaction as well. Post transaction monitoring looks for patterns a single payment cannot show, such as money moving quickly onward through several accounts, and it feeds confirmed fraud back into the scoring model and the velocity rules. A fraud report from a customer triggers a fast recall and beneficiary bank engagement process, with the original payment record preserved and every step logged.

decision.question: A Meridian Bank customer who normally sends small domestic payments suddenly sends a large instant cross-border payment to a new beneficiary, from a new device, late at night. The payment passes sanctions screening. What should the fraud control do?

options.label: A
options.detail: Block the customer account permanently without telling them why.

options.label: B
options.detail: Let it through, since sanctions screening passed.

options.label: C
options.detail: Split the payment into smaller amounts so it looks less risky.

options.label: D
options.detail: Step up the journey with a strong confirmation, show the verified beneficiary name, check velocity and device signals, and hold or challenge the payment where the combined risk exceeds the approved threshold.

decisionRationale: Option D is correct because the combined signals justify friction: step up authentication, confirm the beneficiary, and hold or challenge where the threshold is breached. Option B is wrong because sanctions clearance is not fraud clearance. Option A is wrong because a permanent block without explanation or a defined process is disproportionate and unauditable. Option C is wrong because splitting a payment to evade a control is itself a suspicious act.

steps.title: Logs in and submits an instant payment to a beneficiary
Scores the payment from beneficiary history, amount, velocity, device and behaviour signals
Runs Verification of Payee and shows the verified beneficiary name for confirmation
Confirms the beneficiary, amount and purpose, or completes step up authentication where required
Applies the risk decision: proceed, hold for review, or reject
Reviews a held payment with the signals and score, and records a release or reject decision
Submits a cleared payment to the instant clearing system
Confirms the outcome and starts post transaction monitoring

happy: A customer sends a routine payment to a known beneficiary. The risk score is low, Verification of Payee confirms the name, the customer confirms the amount, screening passes, the payment settles within the instant limit, and the customer sees a confirmed completion with no added friction.

negative.title: High risk new beneficiary
negative.detail: A large payment to a new beneficiary from a new device scores above the threshold. Step up authentication, show the verified beneficiary name, and hold for analyst review where the risk remains high.

negative.title: Authorised push payment scam
negative.detail: The customer is persuaded to send money to a fraudster and confirms the payment themselves. Use the confirmation screen and mismatch warnings as prevention, and on report, start the fast recall process with the beneficiary bank and preserve all evidence.

negative.title: Velocity attack
negative.detail: Many payments leave one account or many accounts in a short window. Apply velocity limits, hold further payments, alert the fraud team, and review the accounts as a linked pattern.

negative.title: Fraud service timeout
negative.detail: The fraud scoring service does not respond within its deadline. Apply the approved fail open or fail closed rule for that control, hold or reject explicitly where required, and record the decision.

technical: Store the risk score, the contributing signals, the threshold applied, the model and rule versions, the Verification of Payee outcome and the customer confirmation as structured data linked by correlation ID. Version the fraud rules and the scoring model with effective dates and record the version used for each payment. Make the decision auditable: the analyst must be able to reconstruct why a payment proceeded, was challenged or was held. Keep the synchronous fraud decision separate from post transaction monitoring, and feed confirmed fraud outcomes back into tuning with a controlled change process. Protect customer and device data under the applicable privacy rules and limit analyst access to what the case needs.

messages.title: Payment status report confirming clearing acceptance or rejection
Internal record of the risk score, signals and decision, not a scheme message

accounting: No ledger posting occurs for a payment held or rejected on fraud grounds; any reservation is released exactly once. A payment released after review posts normally, with the review decision linked to the ledger record. Confirmed fraud creates a linked investigation and recovery case, with any recall or return posted as a separate linked event, never by editing the original payment. Operations monitor fraud detection rates, false positive rates, step up rates, hold ageing and recovery rates, and review thresholds regularly so genuine customers are not over challenged.

scenarios.given: a payment scores above the approved fraud threshold
scenarios.then: the payment is challenged or held for review. the signals and score are recorded

scenarios.given: Verification of Payee returns a name mismatch
scenarios.when: the customer is shown the mismatch
scenarios.then: the customer must explicitly confirm before proceeding. the mismatch is recorded with the payment

questions.question: Why is sanctions clearance not enough to clear a payment for fraud?
options: Sanctions screening checks lists; fraud scoring checks behaviour, velocity, device and beneficiary signals
Sanctions and fraud are the same check
questions.explanation: Sanctions and fraud controls answer different questions and both must run.

questions.question: What should a Verification of Payee mismatch trigger?
options: Nothing, the customer can ignore it
A clear warning and an explicit customer confirmation before proceeding
questions.explanation: A mismatch must be presented clearly with a pause and an explicit confirmation, as the last chance to stop a misdirected or scam payment.

questions.question: What is the right response to a velocity attack across several accounts?
options: Apply velocity limits, hold further payments and review the pattern as linked
questions.explanation: Velocity is a pattern signal, so the response must treat the payments as linked and stop the pattern.

questions.question: Why does post transaction monitoring matter for instant payments?
options: It detects patterns a single payment cannot show, such as money moving quickly onward
It replaces all pre payment checks
Instant payments can always be recalled easily
questions.explanation: Once an instant payment settles, recovery is hard, so post transaction pattern detection and fast recall matter.
